merges.rule: Hurlbut's chapter names 'Gurdon S. Hubbard, Esq. then a youth of sixteen', born Windsor, Vt., 1802, who first arrived at Chicago at the end of October 1818 and in 1828 bought the American Fur Company's entire interest in the trade of Illinois. This project's resident record is Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, graded attested. Three things agree and the surname is the least of them: the given name plus middle initial, where Gurdon S. Hubbard is Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard initial for initial and Gurdon is not a common given name; the town, both being at Chicago; and the TRADE, where the resident record's own occupation note already says he 'supplied Andreas with the Ramsey Crooks correspondence on the early fur trade' and Ramsey Crooks is named on this same page as the company's western manager. A common-name coincidence does not reach three agreements, and there was one Gurdon Hubbard at Chicago.

merges.rule: The American Fur Company's outfit book of 1821 reads 'Consignment to address of Jamie Kinzie for account of him and the American Fur Company; for trade of Milliwaki, to Chicago', and Hurlbut's own bracketed note immediately under it reads 'The late James Kinzie, formerly of Chicago, and half brother of the late John H. Kinzie.' The merge of Jamie Kinzie into James Kinzie is therefore not this project's inference at all: it is the editor's identification, printed on the page beside the entry it explains, and Jamie is the familiar form of James. It carries to this project's resident James Kinzie on the town — 'formerly of Chicago' — and on the kinship, this dataset holding John Harris Kinzie as a separate resident under the name Hurlbut abbreviates to John H. Kinzie.

merges.does_not_follow: The KINSHIP is not written into either household record on this ticket. Hurlbut says half brother, which is a specific and easily-flattened relationship, and adding a family link between two existing households is a change to the residents dataset rather than a reading of a book. It is recorded in bk_afc_015 and proposed in T-0575. Nor does a consignment addressed to a man in 1821 put him anywhere in 1835: hh_kinzie_james.json already dates his arrival from the 1831 ferry bond and this reading does not move it.

merges.rule: Hurlbut's chapter reads 'Mr. John Crafts was a trader sent to Chicago by a Mr. Conant, of Detroit' and, three sentences on, 'Crafts died here of bilious fever in December, of I think the year 1823.' Fergus's obituary of the old settlers prints 'Crafts, John, died 1825.', read into this project as fdn0137 with the normalized name John Crafts. Given name and surname agree in full; both are men named John Crafts who died at Chicago; and both are placed in the town's first trading generation, one by the American Fur Company narrative and the other by inclusion in a list of Chicago's old settlers. Chicago in the early 1820s held a few dozen households and did not hold two John Craftses.
merges.does_not_follow: THE TWO DEATH YEARS ARE NOT RECONCILED AND THIS MERGE DOES NOT PICK ONE. Hubbard says December, 'I think the year 1823', with the hedge in the source's own words; Fergus's printed list says 1825. Both readings stand as filed, the disagreement is the finding, and choosing between them would be inventing a certainty neither source offers. Nothing follows for the town either way: John Crafts was dead at least ten years before the scene date, he is in no resident record, and none is created.

merges.rule: Caroline M. McIlvaine's Introduction calls him 'Gurdon Hubbard' throughout — 'In 1834 Gurdon Hubbard went to Chicago to remain for the rest of his life' — while the title page of the same volume prints Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, and this project's resident record is Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, graded attested. The merge rests on the volume itself and not on a surname: one book, one man, two spellings of him between its covers, with the fuller form on its own title page. Gurdon is not a common given name and the Introduction is explicitly about the subject of the Autobiography.

merges.does_not_follow: It does not follow that anything McIlvaine says about him in 1835 is eyewitness. She is writing in 1911 and Hubbard's own narrative ends in November 1830 (bk_hub_104).

merges.rule: Hubbard writes 'John H. Kinzie' of the Mackinaw clerk of about his own age whose father then resided at Chicago and who gave him letters of introduction to the family. This project's resident record is John Harris Kinzie, graded attested, whose own 1834 advertisement is for 'J. H. Kinzie, forwarding and commission merchant' and who had been Indian sub-agent at Fort Winnebago. Given name, middle initial and surname agree initial for initial; the father at Chicago agrees; and John H. Kinzie is how the man signed himself. A surname alone would be refused here and this is not one.
merges.does_not_follow: It does not follow that he was at Chicago in 1818. Hubbard is explicit that John H. Kinzie 'was stationed permanently at Mackinaw, and was not to be sent into the Indian country'.

merges.rule: Hubbard names 'Robert Kinzie' twice: as 'their youngest son, Robert, late paymaster of the U. S. Army' among the family he met in 1818, and as the man who rose with him and swam the river to the fort fire. This project's resident record is Robert Allen Kinzie, graded attested, named in the 1833 roster as one of 'The Kinzies, John and Robert A., merchants' and recorded by Andreas as the one who remained in Chicago when the rest of the family left in the spring of 1831. Given name plus the same household plus the same generation; the middle name is supplied by this project's record and not contradicted by the book.
merges.does_not_follow: It does not follow that he is placed anywhere in 1835 by this source. Both namings are 1818 and 1827.

merges.rule: The book prints 'Russell E. Heacock' as one of two American families occupying the old log officers' quarters inside the pickets of the ungarrisoned fort in July 1827. This project's resident record is Russel E. Heacock, graded attested, an attorney and justice of the peace who Andreas says 'had come in 1827'. The two spellings differ by one letter in the surname and agree in given name, middle initial and surname otherwise; the arrival year in this project's own record is the year of the book's naming. The one-l and two-l spellings of this surname are both in nineteenth-century print.
merges.does_not_follow: It does not follow that his 1835 dwelling was in the fort. The naming is July 1827, when the fort had no garrison; by 1835 it had.

merges.rule: McIlvaine's list of the town trustees chosen at the election of 11 August 1834 names 'J. S. C. Hogan'. This project's resident record is John S. C. Hogan, graded attested — 'John S. C. Hogan, Postmaster, came in 1832'. Three initials and a surname against a given name and the same three-part sequence, in the same town, in a civic list two years after this project's own record has him arriving. Initials plus a surname would be a refusal if the initials were two; three initials in the same order against the same surname, in a printed list of five trustees, is a match.
merges.does_not_follow: It does not follow that this project may now grade him a trustee. The list is McIlvaine's, written in 1911, and belongs beside the town's own record of the 1834 election and not in front of it.

merges.rule: Hubbard writes that the American Fur Company's round-log storehouse on the river edge, built and occupied by its agent Mr John Craft, 'after the death of Mr. Craft, was occupied by Jean Baptiste Beaubien'. This project's resident record is Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien, graded attested, 'J. B. Beaubien, merchant' in the 1833 roster and a licensed trader on the county court's earliest permits. Given name, both middle names and surname agree in full; the rank is this project's addition and the trade agrees. Hurlbut's chapter makes the same succession from Craft to Beaubien and this project already merged the same man there.
merges.does_not_follow: It does not follow that the storehouse is data/structures/jb_beaubien_homestead.json. Hubbard's building is a round-log Fur Company storehouse on the river edge east of a hewn-log house; that identification is a separate argument and this pass does not make it.

merges.rule: Hubbard names 'Billy Caldwell' as the man who drew Shaub-e-nee's annuity for him, who had Shaub-e-nee as his guest at Chicago the evening before Governor Cass's visit in July 1827, and who was camped with his wife near Yellow Head Point in November 1830. This project's resident record is Billy Caldwell (Sauganash), graded attested, born about 1780 and dying at Chicago in 1841. Given name and surname agree exactly; the parenthesis is this project's own gloss of his Potawatomi name and adds nothing to distinguish; and the association with Shaub-e-nee is in both.
merges.does_not_follow: It does not follow that he is placed at Chicago in 1835. The two namings are 1827 and November 1830, and the November 1830 one puts him camped near the Kankakee, not in the town.

merges.rule: Beckwith's footnote at leaf 375 names 'Billy Caldwell, whose name is so intimately connected with early Chicago', as the husband of Min-ne-mung's sister. This project holds the resident Billy Caldwell (Sauganash), graded attested, interpreter to the United States Indian agency at Chicago under Col. T. J. V. Owen and present on the scene date. Billy Caldwell is Billy Caldwell (Sauganash) with the Potawatomi name dropped, which is how the shorter form is always printed; the merge does not rest on the surname, which would be refused, but on the given name plus the surname plus the town - Beckwith says 'early Chicago' and the resident record says Chicago - plus the ROLE, an intermediary between the agency and the Potawatomi, which is exactly the position a marriage into the Yellow Head's family describes. There is no second Billy Caldwell in this project and none in Beckwith.
merges.what_it_adds: A marriage this project did not hold: Caldwell's wife was the sister of Min-ne-mung (the Yellow Head), whose village stood at Yellow-Head's Point north of Momence on the Kankakee. It changes no placement, no grade and no household.

The same passage names Hubbard's informant's 'brother William' — William Gale — among the passengers of 25 May 1835. This project holds Stephen F. Gale, graded attested. William Gale against Stephen F. Gale is a disagreement of given names on a shared surname and is refused for that reason alone, without reaching the middle initial. REFUSED.

REFUSED.

The same account names 'Mather' as the third purchaser and, further down, says the Chicago Historical Society received the plat by gift of 'one of Mr. Mather's descendants, Judge James H. Roberts'. This project holds no Mather. 'Mather' is a bare surname; Judge James H. Roberts is a descendant writing decades later and not the man. REFUSED on both counts, and recorded because a run reading the Russell & Mather addition will meet this name and should meet this note with it.

This project holds a letter-list resident recorded as William Hunter, graded inferred. David against William is a disagreement of given names on a shared surname. REFUSED.

THIS PROJECT HOLDS NO WOLCOTT HOUSEHOLD. He is set here against Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien only because Beaubien is the nearest thing this project has — the other named man occupying a Fort Dearborn building in the 1820s — and the two are plainly different men with different names and different buildings. REFUSED, and recorded as an absence: Wolcott died in 1830 and belongs to the town before the scene.

Hubbard names 'Mrs. Helm' as John Kinzie's eldest daughter, at the 1818 breakfast table and again crying fire from her window in 1827. She is a surname with a courtesy title, which this domain's rule makes a refusal outright, and this project holds no Helm. REFUSED.

Hubbard names 'Maria' as John Kinzie's youngest daughter, 'now the wife of Major-General David Hunter'; Maria Kinzie is that name with the family surname the sentence gives her. Set against Juliette Augusta Magill Kinzie, the only Kinzie woman this project holds: Maria Kinzie is a daughter of the house and Juliette Augusta Magill Kinzie married John Harris Kinzie in 1830, so they are a sister and a sister-in-law and not one woman. REFUSED, and this project holds no Maria Kinzie.

Hubbard names Shaub-e-nee repeatedly — welcoming him at Bureau Post, absent from the 1827 payment with his annuity drawn by Caldwell, and going into Big Foot's village alone. He is a single name and this project holds no record for him. He is set against Billy Caldwell (Sauganash) because the two are named in the same sentence and both carry a Potawatomi name beside an English one, which is exactly the kind of pairing a careless sweep would collapse. They are two men and the source says so in one breath. REFUSED.

REFUSED, and recorded as an absence rather than a match: the naming is 1818 and nothing here places Ouilmette in 1835.

The shared initial is what makes this pair look like a match and it is worth nothing — the surname agrees, the initial agrees, and the one datum that can separate them separates them absolutely. Nor is there a family route: the same page has H. H. Porter's father Rufus King Porter practising law at Machias 'until his death, in 1856', and his mother dying at Machias in 1862, so no near relative of this H. Porter was in Illinois at all in 1835.

H. Porter of this autobiography. Three things say so and any one of them would be enough: the given names do not agree (Jeremiah against Henry Hobart), the trade does not agree (a minister against a railway clerk who became a banker and stockyard promoter), and the dates make it impossible — H. The autobiography names no minister among its relations and never mentions Jeremiah Porter.
